newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Turkmenistan protests over Russian-Azeri oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Turkmenistan protests over Russian-Azeri oil deal.

text.p: Turkmenistan reacted angrily on Saturday to a Russian-Azeri oil deal on a major field in the Caspian Sea by calling in Moscow's ambassador and demanding the agreement be annulled.

Azerbaijan's state oil company SOCAR signed a $1 billion preliminary agreement on Friday with the Russian state oil company Rosneft and the largest oil company in Russia, LUKoil, to develop the Kyapaz field.
It is estimated to hold more than 50 million tonnes.
"We cannot but be surprised, to say the least, by the decision adopted by Russia and Azerbaijan with regard to the oil field," a Turkmen Foreign Ministry statement said.
"Turkmenistan's rights to this deposit are obvious and cannot be a matter for ambiguous interpretation."

Turkmenistan, which like Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Iran is one of the Caspian Sea's littoral states, refers to the Kyapaz field as Serdar. The field lies in the far south of the Caspian, between Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan.

The statement was faxed to Reuters by the Turkmenistan embassy in Moscow. In a separate statement, the embassy said Russia's ambassador to Ashgabat, Vadim Cherepov, had been called in and handed a "strong protest".

"The Foreign Ministry of Turkmenistan is authorised to express a strong protest in connection with this development and to demand categorically that the agreement must be annulled to avoid consequences for which Turkmenistan will not bear any responsibility," the ministry statement said.
Ashgabat wanted littoral states to boost efforts to reach an agreement on how to carve up the oil-rich Caspian Sea, the embassy said.

There was no immediate comment from Russian or Azeri officials. Azerbaijan's president, Haydar Aliyev, visited Moscow this week for talks with Russian President Boris Yeltsin and ministers on oil and other bilateral matters.
Much of the debate over the Caspian Sea hinges on whether it is designated a sea or lake. International boundaries would be drawn differently in each case.
With tens of millions of tonnes of oil, the economic development of five countries and the interests of multinational oil companies at stake, the diplomatic wrangling is particularly intense.

Moscow has argued that the Caspian is a salt lake whose oil resources should be developed jointly by the five surrounding states. Others have said it should be viewed as a sea, and each of the five should have a separate share of the riches.
